answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 15.

answer.text:
This is an **NMOS cascode gain stage**: \(M_1\) is common-source and \(M_2\) is common-gate. The ideal source \(I_1\) supplies a constant bias current and is an **AC open circuit**.

Assume low-frequency small-signal operation, both MOSFETs in saturation, \(V_{b1}\) AC-grounded, and finite \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\) due to channel-length modulation. Define

\[
g_{o1}=\frac1{r_{o1}},\qquad g_{o2}=\frac1{r_{o2}},\qquad 
G_2=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}
\]

where \(g_{mb2}\) is the body-effect transconductance of \(M_2\). If body effect is ignored, set \(g_{mb2}=0\).

---

## 1. DC bias and headroom

At the bias point,

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1.
\]

The intermediate node is approximately

\[
V_X=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}
=V_{b1}-\big[V_{TH2}(V_X)+V_{OV2}\big],
\]

where body effect may raise \(V_{TH2}\) because \(V_{SB2}=V_X\).

Saturation requires

\[
V_X\ge V_{OV1},
\]

\[
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_X+V_{OV2},
\]

and the upper output voltage is limited by the headroom of the current-source load:

\[
V_{\text{out}}\le V_{DD}-V_{\text{headroom},I_1}.
\]

Thus, with \(V_X\approx V_{OV1}\), the minimum allowed output voltage is roughly

\[
V_{\text{out,min}}\approx V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}.
\]

The cascode gives high gain but costs one extra overdrive voltage of output swing.

---

## 2. Small-signal gain

For \(M_1\),

\[
i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{o1}v_x.
\]

For \(M_2\), with gate and body AC-grounded,

\[
i_{d2}=g_{o2}(v_{\text{out}}-v_x)-G_2v_x.
\]

Because \(I_1\) is ideal, its incremental current is zero. Therefore,

\[
i_{d2}=0,\qquad i_{d1}=i_{d2}=0.
\]

From \(M_1\),

\[
g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{o1}v_x=0
\]

so

\[
v_x=-g_{m1}r_{o1}v_{in}.
\]

From \(M_2\),

\[
g_{o2}(v_{\text{out}}-v_x)-G_2v_x=0,
\]

giving

\[
v_{\text{out}}=\left[1+G_2r_{o2}\right]v_x.
\]

Therefore the voltage gain is

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{in}}
=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]
}
\]

or, neglecting body effect,

\[
\boxed{
A_v=-g_{m1}r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})
}
\]

and for \(g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg1\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}.
}
\]

If both devices have the same \(g_m\) and \(r_o\),

\[
A_v\approx -(g_mr_o)^2.
\]

Thus the cascode gain is approximately the **product of two intrinsic gains**, rather than the single \(g_mr_o\) of a simple common-source stage. The stage is inverting.

---

## 3. Output resistance

With \(v_{in}=0\), applying a test voltage at the output gives

\[
R_{\text{out,cascode}}
=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+G_2r_{o1}r_{o2}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out,cascode}}
=r_{o2}+r_{o1}\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]
}
\]

and for \(G_2r_{o2}\gg1\),

\[
R_{\text{out,cascode}}\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}.
\]

A more exact Norton representation is

\[
i_o=G_m v_{in}+\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{R_{\text{out,cascode}}},
\]

with

\[
G_m
=g_{m1}\frac{G_2+g_{o2}}
{g_{o1}+G_2+g_{o2}}
\approx g_{m1}.
\]

If the practical current-source load has finite output resistance \(r_{oI}\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v\approx -G_m\left(R_{\text{out,cascode}}\parallel r_{oI}\right)
}
\]

so a non-cascoded current-source load can limit the achievable gain.

---

## 4. Important limiting case

The finite gain above relies on finite \(r_{o1}\) and \(r_{o2}\). If channel-length modulation is neglected entirely, \(r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty\), and with an ideal current source the output voltage is not well defined; the small-signal gain tends to infinity. In a real circuit, device output resistance, current-source compliance, or a finite load resistance sets the gain.

In summary: the circuit is a high-output-resistance, inverting cascode amplifier with

\[
A_v\approx -(g_mr_o)^2,
\]

at the cost of reduced output swing and an extra bias voltage \(V_{b1}\).

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 15.

answer.text:
This is an **NMOS cascode common-source amplifier**: \(M_1\) converts \(v_{in}\) into a small-signal current, while \(M_2\), biased as a common-gate device, transfers this current to the output and isolates node \(X\) from output-voltage variations. The current source \(I_1\) is an ideal, high-resistance load.

Assume low-frequency operation, both MOSFETs in saturation, \(V_{DD}\) and \(V_{b1}\) at ac ground, and define

\[
g_{oi}=\frac{1}{r_{oi}},\qquad
g_t=g_{m2}+g_{mb2},
\]

where \(g_{mb2}\) accounts for body effect in \(M_2\). Set \(g_{mb2}=0\) if body effect is neglected.

## DC operation

Both transistors carry the bias current:

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1.
\]

Also,

\[
V_X=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}.
\]

For saturation,

\[
V_X\ge V_{OV1},\qquad
V_{out}-V_X\ge V_{OV2},
\]

or equivalently

\[
V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}.
\]

With the usual minimum bias \(V_{b1}=V_{GS2}+V_{OV1}\), the minimum output voltage is approximately

\[
V_{out,\min}\approx V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}.
\]

A practical current-source load also imposes an upper output-swing limit set by its headroom.

## Midband voltage gain

The small-signal drain currents are

\[
i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{o1}v_X,
\]

\[
i_{d2}=g_{o2}v_{out}-(g_t+g_{o2})v_X.
\]

Since \(I_1\) is ideal, its incremental current is zero. Hence, with no output load,

\[
i_{d2}=0,
\]

and KCL at \(X\) gives \(i_{d1}=i_{d2}=0\). Therefore,

\[
v_X=-g_{m1}r_{o1}v_{in},
\]

and

\[
v_{out}=(1+g_t r_{o2})v_X.
\]

Thus the exact low-frequency gain, including \(r_o\) effects, is

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]
}
\]

or, neglecting body effect,

\[
\boxed{
A_v=-g_{m1}r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})
\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}.
}
\]

For identical devices this is approximately

\[
A_v\approx -(g_mr_o)^2,
\]

i.e. a gain on the order of the square of the intrinsic device gain. The stage is inverting.

## Output resistance and Norton form

With \(v_{in}=0\), the resistance looking into the cascode output is

\[
\boxed{
R_o=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_t r_{o1}r_{o2}
\approx g_t r_{o1}r_{o2}.
}
\]

The exact short-circuit transconductance of the complete cascode is

\[
G_m=
g_{m1}\frac{g_t+g_{o2}}
{g_{o1}+g_t+g_{o2}}
\approx g_{m1}.
\]

Hence, for any finite load \(R_L\),

\[
\boxed{
A_v=-G_m(R_o\parallel R_L)
\approx -g_{m1}(R_o\parallel R_L).
}
\]

If \(I_1\) has finite output resistance \(r_{oI}\), use \(R_L=r_{oI}\) in this expression. If \(R_L\ll R_o\), the gain reduces to approximately \(-g_{m1}R_L\); thus a cascode increases gain only when the load resistance is also high.

Many first-order treatments use \(G_m\simeq g_{m1}\) even for an ideal load and write

\[
A_v\simeq -g_{m1}R_o
=-g_{m1}(r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_t r_{o1}r_{o2}).
\]

This differs from the exact result by the lower-order term \(g_{m1}r_{o2}\); both give the same dominant term \(-g_{m1}g_t r_{o1}r_{o2}\).

## Main properties

- \(R_{in}\to\infty\) at low frequency, since the input is an MOS gate.
- Output resistance is boosted from roughly \(r_o\) to roughly \(g_mr_o^2\).
- Node \(X\) has a relatively low impedance, about \(1/g_t\), reducing Miller multiplication of \(M_1\)'s \(C_{gd}\) and improving bandwidth.
- The dominant pole is normally at the high-resistance output node.
- If channel-length modulation is neglected entirely (\(r_o\to\infty\)), both the output resistance and ideal-load gain tend to infinity, and the DC output voltage is not well defined. Finite \(r_o\) is therefore essential to the finite result.

**No—not as a functional cascode.**

Let \(X\) be the junction of \(M_1\) and \(M_2\). The arrows indicate that \(M_1\) is NMOS and \(M_2\) is PMOS. With a positive \(V_{DD}\), current flows downward, so for \(M_2\):

- \(X\) is its **drain**.

Thus \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are connected **drain-to-drain**. A true cascode requires

\[
D_{M_1} \rightarrow S_{M_2},\qquad V_{\text{out}}=D_{M_2},
\]

so that \(M_2\) is a common-gate current buffer shielding \(M_1\)'s drain from output variations. Here the signal enters \(M_2\)'s drain and exits at its source—the common-gate path is reversed. Consequently, there is no cascode output-resistance multiplication; the output is a source terminal with roughly \(1/g_m\)-scale resistance in parallel with \(R_D\).

If \(M_2\) were an NMOS oriented with its source at \(X\) and its drain at \(V_{\text{out}}\), the circuit would be a conventional cascode.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect is reduced in a cascode because the **large voltage gain is not developed across the input transistor’s feedback capacitance**.

Consider the lower transistor in a cascode: common-emitter/common-source device, followed by a common-base/common-gate device. The troublesome capacitance is the lower device’s \(C_{bc}\) or \(C_{gd}\), between the input node and its collector/drain node.

By Miller’s theorem, a capacitance \(C_f\) between input and another node with voltage gain \(A_x = v_x/v_{in}\) appears at the input as

\[
C_{in} = C_f(1 - A_x).
\]

In an ordinary common-emitter/common-source stage, the collector/drain has large negative gain:

\[
A_x \approx -g_m R_L,
\]

so

\[
C_{in} \approx C_f(1+g_m R_L),
\]

which can be very large. That is the Miller effect.

In a cascode, however, the lower transistor’s collector/drain is connected to the emitter/source of the upper transistor. That node has a low impedance, roughly \(1/g_m\), so its voltage swing is small. The gain from the input to this intermediate node is only about

\[
A_x \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx -1
\]

for similar devices. Therefore the Miller multiplication is only about

\[
C_{in} \approx C_f(1+1) \approx 2C_f,
\]

rather than being multiplied by the full amplifier gain.

The upper transistor’s collector/drain may have a large output swing, but that node is isolated from the input transistor by the common-base/common-gate device. Thus the large output voltage gain does not appear across the lower transistor’s \(C_{bc}/C_{gd}\).

So, in short: **a cascode holds the lower transistor’s collector/drain voltage nearly constant and shifts the large voltage swing to the upper device, greatly reducing Miller feedback capacitance and improving high-frequency bandwidth.**

The approximate −1 local gain is a minor modeling variation from the golden solution’s roughly −2, not a change to the essential reasoning.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
The Miller effect is reduced in a cascode because the high-gain output node is isolated from the input node.

For a capacitance \(C\) between an input node and a node with voltage gain \(A_v=v_2/v_1\), the effective input capacitance is

\[
C_{\text{in}} = C(1-A_v)
\]

For an inverting common-source/common-emitter stage, \(A_v\) is large and negative, so

\[
C_{\text{in}} \approx C(1+|A_v|)
\]

which can be very large.

In a cascode, however:

- The input transistor’s drain/collector is not the final high-swing output node.
- It is connected to the source/emitter of the cascode transistor, whose gate/base is AC-grounded.
- Looking into that source/emitter is a low impedance, roughly \(1/g_m\).
- Therefore the voltage gain from the input to this intermediate node is small:

\[
\frac{v_x}{v_i} \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}
\]

often only about \(-1\).

So the \(C_{gd}\) or \(C_{bc}\) of the input device is Miller-multiplied only by a small factor, e.g.

\[
C_{\text{in}} \approx C_{gd1}\left(1+\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}\right)
\]

rather than by the full amplifier gain.

Meanwhile, the large output swing occurs at the upper transistor’s drain/collector, but that node is shielded from the input. The upper device’s gate/base is AC-grounded, so its \(C_{gd}\) or \(C_{bc}\) mostly appears as capacitance to ground at the output, not as Miller capacitance at the input.

Thus, a cascode still provides high gain, but the high-gain output node is not directly capacitively coupled to the input node, so the Miller effect is much less pronounced.

For a capacitance \(C_f\) between an input node and a node with gain \(A_v=v_x/v_i\), Miller’s theorem gives

\[
C_{\text{in}} = C_f(1-A_v)
\]

\[

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
Assume ideal bias sources \(V_{b1}\), \(V_{b2}\), so \(V_{DD}\), both gates, and the bodies are at ac ground. Also assume both devices are initially in saturation. No numerical device parameters are given, so the result is symbolic.

## 1. Circuit identification and dc operation

- \(M_1\) is a PMOS current-source load: source at \(V_{DD}\), gate at \(V_{b2}\), drain at \(V_{\text{out}}\).
- \(M_2\) is an NMOS common-gate device: drain at \(V_{\text{out}}\), gate at \(V_{b1}\), source at \(V_{\text{in}}\).
- Since the gate of \(M_2\) is fixed, the circuit is non-inverting.

Let

\[
\beta_i=\mu_i C_{\rm ox}(W/L)_i,
\]

\[
V_{OVp}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{Tp}|,
\qquad
V_{OVn}=V_{b1}-V_{\text{in},Q}-V_{Tn}.
\]

Ignoring channel-length modulation initially,

\[
I_{P0}=\frac{\beta_p}{2}V_{OVp}^{2},
\qquad
I_{N0}=\frac{\beta_n}{2}V_{OVn}^{2},
\]

and dc equilibrium requires \(I_{P0}=I_{N0}=I_Q\). Thus

\[
V_{\text{in},Q}
=
V_{b1}-V_{Tn}
-\sqrt{\frac{2I_{P0}}{\beta_n}}.
\]

With channel-length modulation,

\[
I_{P0}\!\left[1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out},Q})\right]
=
I_{N0}\!\left[1+\lambda_n(V_{\text{out},Q}-V_{\text{in},Q})\right],
\]

which determines \(V_{\text{out},Q}\). If both \(\lambda\)'s are neglected, the current equality fixes \(V_{\text{in},Q}\) but does not fix \(V_{\text{out},Q}\): the output node is floating between two ideal current sources. A finite output conductance, output load, or triode-region operation is needed to establish the dc output voltage.

### Saturation and output swing

\[
M_2\text{ saturated:}\qquad
V_{\text{out}}\ge V_{b1}-V_{Tn},
\]

\[
M_1\text{ saturated:}\qquad
V_{\text{out}}\le V_{b2}+|V_{Tp}|.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
V_{b1}-V_{Tn}
\le V_{\text{out}}\le
V_{b2}+|V_{Tp}|
}
\]

or, at the bias point,

\[
\boxed{
V_{\text{in},Q}+V_{OVn}
\le V_{\text{out}}\le
V_{DD}-V_{OVp}
}.
\]

Body effect makes \(V_{Tn}\) depend on \(V_{SB}\), so \(V_{Tn,Q}\) should be used.

---

## 2. Small-signal voltage gain

Define

\[
G_m=g_{m2}+g_{mb2},
\qquad
g_{o1}=\frac1{r_{o1}},
\qquad
g_{o2}=\frac1{r_{o2}},
\]

where \(g_{mb2}\) accounts for body effect. If the body of \(M_2\) is tied to its source, or if \(\gamma=0\), set \(g_{mb2}=0\).

Since \(M_1\)'s gate and source are both at ac ground, its \(g_m\) does not contribute; it appears only as \(r_{o1}\). The output-node KCL is

\[
\frac{v_o}{r_{o1}}
+\frac{v_o-v_i}{r_{o2}}
-G_m v_i=0.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
A_v\equiv\frac{v_o}{v_i}
=
\frac{G_m+1/r_{o2}}
{1/r_{o1}+1/r_{o2}}
=
\left(G_m+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)
(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
}
\]

or

\[
A_v
=
G_m(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
+\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}.
\]

Since \(G_m r_{o2}\gg1\) normally,

\[
\boxed{
A_v \simeq (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
}
\]

and the gain is positive. Physically, a positive source-voltage increment reduces the current sunk by \(M_2\); the PMOS load then charges the output node, so \(V_{\text{out}}\) rises.

Useful limits are

\[
r_{o1}\ll r_{o2}:\quad A_v\simeq G_m r_{o1},
\]

\[
r_{o1}\gg r_{o2}:\quad A_v\simeq 1+G_m r_{o2}.
\]

If an external load \(R_L\) is present, replace \(r_{o1}\) in the load branch by

\[
R_X=r_{o1}\parallel R_L,
\]

giving

\[
A_v=\left(G_m+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)(r_{o2}\parallel R_X).
\]

If both \(r_{o1}\) and \(r_{o2}\) are taken as infinite, the gain and dc output voltage are undefined/infinite; with only output capacitance, the circuit behaves as an integrator rather than a finite-gain amplifier.

---

## 3. Input resistance

The input current at the source is

\[
i_i=G_m v_i+\frac{v_i-v_o}{r_{o2}}.
\]

Using the gain above,

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}
=
\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}
{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}
=
\frac{r_{o1}}{A_v}
}
\]

for no external load. With \(R_L\), replace \(r_{o1}\) by \(R_X=r_{o1}\parallel R_L\).

In the usual approximation where the output load resistance is much smaller than \(r_{o2}\),

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}\simeq
\frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}
\simeq \frac1{g_{m2}}
}.
\]

For a very high-resistance PMOS current source, \(R_{\text{in}}\) can be appreciably larger than \(1/g_m\); for \(r_{o1}\rightarrow\infty\), the ideal small-signal model gives \(R_{\text{in}}\rightarrow\infty\).

---

## 4. Output resistance

With the input voltage source set to zero, the source, gate, and body of \(M_2\) are at ac ground. Thus

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}
}
\]

or \(r_{o2}\parallel(r_{o1}\parallel R_L)\) with an external load.

If the input is driven through a finite source resistance \(R_S\), the resistance looking into the drain of \(M_2\) is increased by source degeneration:

\[
r_{o,\text{M2}}
\simeq
r_{o2}+R_S+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}R_S,
\]

so

\[
R_{\text{out}}
=
(r_{o1}\parallel R_L)\parallel r_{o,\text{M2}}.
\]

---

## 5. Main characteristics

- **Non-inverting voltage gain**, positive \(A_v\).
- **High output resistance**, set mainly by the two transistor output resistances.
- **Low-to-moderate input resistance**, approximately \(1/g_m\) in the usual approximation.
- **Wide bandwidth:** the gate of \(M_2\) is at ac ground, so \(C_{gd}\) is not Miller-multiplied. The dominant output pole is approximately

\[
\omega_{p,o}\simeq
\frac{1}{(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})C_{\text{out}}}.
\]

- **Bias sensitivity:** without channel-length modulation or an output load, the PMOS and NMOS currents must match exactly and \(V_{\text{out},Q}\) is not defined. Finite output conductance is essential for a practical linear operating point.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the PMOS-loaded NMOS common-gate stage, places Vin at M2’s source, and describes the bias nodes, non-inverting gain, and low input resistance. Its gain expression is equivalent to the required approximation; the additional detail does not contradict the core analysis.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
## 1. Topology and DC conditions

- \(M_2\) is an NMOS **common-gate** device: its gate is held at \(V_{b1}\), the input is applied to its source, and its drain is \(V_{\text{out}}\).
- \(M_1\) is a PMOS **current-source load**: its source/body are at \(V_{DD}\) and its gate is held at \(V_{b2}\).
- \(V_{DD},V_{b1},V_{b2}\) are ac grounds.
- Assume both devices are in saturation and there is no external output load.

Let

\[
V_{OV1}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TP}|,\qquad
V_{OV2}=V_{b1}-V_{\text{in}}-V_{TN}(V_{SB2})
\]

where body effect in \(M_2\) is included in \(V_{TN}\). At dc,

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2},
\]

and the saturation/headroom requirement is

\[
V_{\text{in}}+V_{OV2}\leq V_{\text{out}}
\leq V_{DD}-V_{OV1}.
\]

If channel-length modulation is neglected, \(I_{D1}\) and \(I_{D2}\) are independent of \(V_{\text{out}}\). Thus \(I_{D1}=I_{D2}\) fixes the dc value of \(V_{\text{in}}\), but leaves \(V_{\text{out}}\) undetermined within the saturation interval. Finite output conductance—or a dc feedback path—is therefore necessary for a well-defined small-signal operating point.

---

## 2. Low-frequency small-signal model

Define

\[
G \equiv g_{m2}+g_{mb2},\qquad
g_{o1}=\frac{1}{r_{o1}},\qquad
g_{o2}=\frac{1}{r_{o2}},
\]

where \(r_{o1}\) belongs to the PMOS load and \(r_{o2}\) to the NMOS. If body effect is neglected, set \(g_{mb2}=0\).

The PMOS \(g_{m1}\) does not enter the result because its gate, source, and body are all at ac ground; it contributes only \(g_{o1}\).

For \(M_2\),

\[
i_{d2}=g_{o2}(v_o-v_i)-Gv_i
      =g_{o2}v_o-(G+g_{o2})v_i .
\]

KCL at the output node gives

\[
g_{o1}v_o+i_{d2}=0,
\]

hence

\[
(g_{o1}+g_{o2})v_o=(G+g_{o2})v_i.
\]

### Voltage gain

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_o}{v_i}
=\frac{G+g_{o2}}{g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
=(G+g_{o2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
}
\]

or equivalently,

\[
\boxed{
A_v=
\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}
\left(1+G r_{o2}\right)
}
\]

and, when \(G\gg g_{o2}\),

\[
A_v\simeq G(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}).
\]

The gain is **positive**: increasing \(V_{\text{in}}\) raises the source of \(M_2\), reduces its \(V_{GS}\), reduces its pull-down current, and the PMOS load pulls \(V_{\text{out}}\) upward.

---

## 3. Input resistance

The current entering the source of \(M_2\) is

\[
i_i=-i_{d2}=(G+g_{o2})v_i-g_{o2}v_o.
\]

Using the output-node equation,

\[
i_i=g_{o1}v_o.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}
=\frac{v_i}{i_i}
=\frac{g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
       {g_{o1}(G+g_{o2})}
=\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}{1+G r_{o2}}
}
\]

For an ordinary low-resistance load, \(r_{o1}\ll r_{o2}\), this reduces to the familiar

\[
R_{\text{in}}\simeq \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}.
\]

With a nearly ideal PMOS current-source load, \(r_{o1}\to\infty\), the input resistance can become very large because \(V_{\text{out}}\) moves so as to keep the current through \(M_2\) almost constant.

---

## 4. Output resistance

With \(v_i=0\), i.e. the input driven by an ideal voltage source set to zero, both \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) simply contribute their output conductances:

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}
=\frac{1}{g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
}
\]

If the source of \(M_2\) is instead connected to ground through a source resistance \(R_S\),

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}
=
r_{o1}\parallel
\left[r_{o2}+R_S+G r_{o2}R_S\right]
}
\]

and the gain from a Thevenin source \(v_s\) is

\[
\frac{v_o}{v_s}
=
A_v\frac{R_{\text{in}}}{R_S+R_{\text{in}}}.
\]

If the input port is left open, \(R_S\to\infty\), and \(R_{\text{out}}\to r_{o1}\).

---

## 5. Equal-output-resistance case

If both transistors carry the same current and have similar \(\lambda\), take

\[
r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_o,\qquad G r_o\gg1.
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{1+G r_o}{2}\simeq \frac{G r_o}{2}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{in}}=\frac{2r_o}{1+G r_o}
\simeq \frac{2}{G}
}
\]

\[
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}\simeq \frac{r_o}{2}
}
\]

Thus the current-source load gives a large, non-inverting voltage gain, but the linear output swing is limited by the saturation headroom of the two devices. If \(\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\), the small-signal gain is not finite; channel-length modulation or another output conductance is essential for a meaningful linear analysis.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate NMOS with source input and PMOS current-source load, gives the non-inverting gain with appropriate finite-ro/body-effect refinements, and describes the low input resistance in the usual finite-load case. The ideal-load caveat does not undermine the essential analysis.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
Assume \(V_{DD},V_{b1},V_{b2}\) are ideal dc sources and hence ac grounds, and both transistors operate in saturation.

- \(M_1\): PMOS current-source load; since \(v_{sg1}=0\), only its output resistance \(r_{o1}\) appears in the small-signal circuit.
- \(M_2\): NMOS common-gate device; its source is driven by \(v_{in}\), its gate is ac grounded, and its drain is \(v_{out}\).

Define
\[
G_2=g_{m2}+g_{mb2},\qquad g_{oi}=\frac1{r_{oi}},
\]
where \(g_{mb2}\) is omitted if body effect is neglected or the body is tied to the source.

## DC operating point

At quiescence,
\[
I_{D2}=I_{D1}=I_D.
\]

Using a square-law model,
\[
I_{D2}\simeq \frac12 k_{n2}V_{OV2}^2
 \left[1+\lambda_2(V_{out,Q}-V_{in,Q})\right],
\]
\[
I_{D1}\simeq \frac12 k_{p1}V_{OV1}^2
 \left[1+\lambda_1(V_{DD}-V_{out,Q})\right],
\]
with
\[
V_{OV2}=V_{b1}-V_{in,Q}-V_{Tn}(V_{SB2}),\qquad
V_{OV1}=V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{Tp}|.
\]

Equating these currents determines \(V_{out,Q}\). Both devices remain saturated when
\[
V_{in,Q}+V_{OV2}\le V_{out,Q}\le V_{DD}-V_{OV1}.
\]

If both \(\lambda\)'s are neglected, any current mismatch drives the output toward a supply rail; if the currents are exactly equal, the output voltage is not defined by the ideal model. Finite output resistance is therefore needed for a meaningful small-signal bias point.

## Small-signal voltage gain

For \(M_2\),
\[
v_{gs2}=v_{bs2}=-v_{in},\qquad v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{in}.
\]

Thus the current leaving the output node through \(M_2\) is
\[
i_{d2}=g_{o2}(v_{out}-v_{in})-G_2v_{in}.
\]

The PMOS contributes \(g_{o1}v_{out}\). Output-node KCL gives
\[
g_{o1}v_{out}+g_{o2}(v_{out}-v_{in})-G_2v_{in}=0,
\]
hence
\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=\frac{G_2+g_{o2}}{g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
=(G_2+g_{o2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
}
\]
or equivalently
\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{r_{o1}\left(1+G_2r_{o2}\right)}
{r_{o1}+r_{o2}} }.
\]

Usually \(G_2r_{o2}\gg1\), so
\[
\boxed{A_v\simeq (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})}.
\]

Without body effect,
\[
A_v\simeq g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}).
\]

If channel-length modulation is retained only for \(M_1\), \(r_{o2}\rightarrow\infty\), giving
\[
A_v\simeq (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}.
\]

The gain is **positive/non-inverting**: increasing \(V_{in}\) reduces \(V_{GS2}\) and, through body effect, raises \(V_{T2}\), reducing \(M_2\)'s current. The PMOS then charges the output node upward until current balance is restored.

## Input resistance

The low-frequency input current is
\[
i_{in}=g_{o1}v_{out},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{
R_{in}=\frac{v_{in}}{i_{in}}
=\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}{1+G_2r_{o2}}
=\frac{r_{o1}}{A_v}
}.
\]

For \(G_2r_{o2}\gg1\),
\[
R_{in}\simeq \frac{1}{G_2}\left(1+\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o2}}\right).
\]

If \(r_{o2}\to\infty\), this reduces to the familiar
\[
R_{in}\simeq\frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}},
\]
and body effect lowers the input resistance.

## Output resistance

With the ideal input voltage source set to zero, the source of \(M_2\) is ac grounded; all controlled current sources are inactive. Therefore
\[
\boxed{R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}}.
\]

If the input is driven through a finite source resistance \(R_S\),
\[
R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel
\left[r_{o2}+(1+G_2r_{o2})R_S\right].
\]

For an additional resistive load \(R_L\), replace \(r_{o1}\) everywhere by \(r_{o1}\parallel R_L\). If a capacitance \(C_L\) dominates the output, the approximate output pole is
\[
\omega_p\simeq \frac{g_{o1}+g_{o2}}{C_L}.
\]

Thus the circuit is a noninverting common-gate amplifier with low input resistance, high output resistance, and large gain set mainly by \(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}\) times the parallel output resistances.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate NMOS with PMOS current-source load, the source-driven input and biasing, non-inverting gain, low input resistance, and the expected gain expression. The additional small-signal analysis is consistent with the topology.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit of Figure 18 have?

answer.text:
**Two poles** (for finite \(R_S\)).

All dc bias and supply terminals are ac grounds, so

\[
C_o=C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}
\]

appears from the output node to ground. The only independent dynamic node voltages are:

1. the gate/input node of \(M_1\), and  
2. the common drain/output node.

Although \(C_{GD}\) is an additional capacitor between these nodes, its voltage is simply \(v_i-v_o\); it does not introduce a third independent state. Thus the network determinant is second order. \(C_{GD}\) also produces a feedforward (right-half-plane) zero, but no extra pole.

If \(R_S=0\), the input node is clamped by the ideal source and only one pole remains.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies two independent dynamic nodes and recognizes that the inter-node CGD affects the network without adding a third state. The output shunt capacitances and finite-RS qualification are consistent with the circuit.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit of Figure 18 have?

answer.text:
**Two poles** (assuming finite \(R_S\)).

In the small-signal circuit, all dc bias supplies are ac grounds. Thus

\[
C_{DB},\quad C_{GD2},\quad C_{DB2}
\]

are effectively in parallel from \(V_{\text{out}}\) to ground:

\[
C_o=C_{DB}+C_{GD2}+C_{DB2}.
\]

Only two independent dynamic nodes remain:

- the gate/input node of \(M_1\), with \(C_{GS}\) to ground and \(C_{GD}\) to the output;
- the common drain/output node, with \(C_o\) to ground.

Hence the network determinant is second order in \(s\), giving one input pole and one output pole. \(C_{GD}\) can also introduce a zero, but not another pole.

If \(R_S=0\), the input node is constrained by an ideal voltage source and one pole moves to infinity, leaving one finite pole.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies two dynamic nodes, so the circuit has two poles. It keeps CGD as a coupling capacitance between the input and output nodes rather than treating it as a separate pole; the finite-RS qualification is also reasonable.

answers.question: How many poles does the circuit of Figure 18 have?

answer.text:
The circuit has **two poles** (assuming finite \(R_S\) and ideal dc bias sources).

When the dc sources are set to zero, the gate, source/body bias terminals of \(M_2\) are at ac ground. Thus

\[
C_{GD2},\; C_{DB2},\; C_{DB}
\]

are effectively in parallel from \(V_{\text{out}}\) to ground. The only independent dynamic node voltages are:

1. the gate node of \(M_1\), and  
2. the output/drain node.

Equivalently, the capacitive energy is determined by only two independent voltages, \(v_x\) and \(v_{\text{out}}\):

\[
E_C=\tfrac12 C_{GS}v_x^2
+\tfrac12 C_{GD}(v_x-v_{\text{out}})^2
+\tfrac12(C_{DB}+C_{DB2}+C_{GD2})v_{\text{out}}^2 .
\]

Hence the characteristic equation is second order: one pole is associated mainly with the input node and one with the output node. \(C_{GD}\) can introduce a zero, but not an additional pole.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies two independent dynamic nodes and a second-order response. It accounts for the cross-node CGD and the output-node capacitances without inventing an extra CGS2 load.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
## 1. Ideal long-channel operation

Assume \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) are identical, their bodies are grounded, and initially neglect body effect, channel-length modulation, and leakage. Define

\[
\beta=\mu_n C_{\rm ox}\frac WL,\qquad
v\equiv V_{\rm in}-V_T,\qquad
D\equiv V_{\rm out},
\]

and let \(V_X\) be the source of \(M_2\) / drain of \(M_1\).

For one transistor,

\[
I_D=\beta\left[(V_{GS}-V_T)V_{DS}-\frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right]
\]

in triode.

Since

\[
V_{GS1}-V_T=v,\qquad V_{GS2}-V_T=v-V_X,
\]

conduction of \(M_2\) requires \(V_X<v\). Consequently \(V_{DS1}=V_X<v\), so \(M_1\) is always in triode whenever current flows. The upper transistor is

\[
\begin{cases}
\text{triode}, & D<v,\\
\text{saturation}, & D\ge v,
\end{cases}
\]

because \(M_2\) saturates when

\[
D-V_X\ge v-V_X \iff D\ge v.
\]

Thus both devices can never be saturated simultaneously in this tied-gate stack.

The two currents are

\[
I_1=\frac{\beta}{2}\left[v^2-(v-V_X)^2\right],
\]

\[
I_2=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\beta}{2}\left[(v-V_X)^2-(v-D)^2\right],&D<v,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{\beta}{2}(v-V_X)^2,&D\ge v.
\end{cases}
\]

Equating \(I_1=I_2\) gives

\[
v-V_X=
\begin{cases}
\sqrt{\dfrac{v^2+(v-D)^2}{2}},&D<v,\\[3mm]
\dfrac{v}{\sqrt2},&D\ge v.
\end{cases}
\]

Hence the current through the stack is

\[
\boxed{
I_D=
\begin{cases}
0, & V_{\rm in}\le V_T,\\[1mm]
\dfrac{\beta}{4}\left(2vD-D^2\right), & 0\le D<v,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{\beta}{4}v^2, & D\ge v.
\end{cases}}
\]

This is exactly the square-law characteristic of one NMOS having

\[
\boxed{\beta_{\rm eq}=\frac{\beta}{2}
      =\mu_n C_{\rm ox}\frac{W}{2L}}
\]

or, equivalently,

\[
\boxed{L_{\rm eq}=2L}.
\]

Thus the series pair acts as a single transistor with twice the channel length. Its threshold is still \(V_T\), not \(2V_T\). In the saturation region, \(M_2\) is saturated while \(M_1\) operates in triode, and

\[
V_X=v\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right).
\]

For unequal devices, neglecting body effect,

\[
\frac{1}{\beta_{\rm eq}}=\frac{1}{\beta_1}+\frac{1}{\beta_2},
\]

and for equal widths \(L_{\rm eq}=L_1+L_2\).

---

## 2. Load-line and voltage-transfer characteristic

The resistor imposes

\[
I_D=\frac{V_{DD}-D}{R_D}.
\]

Let

\[
A=\frac{\beta R_D}{4}.
\]

### Off region

For \(V_{\rm in}\le V_T\),

\[
\boxed{V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}}.
\]

### Stack saturated

For \(V_{\rm in}>V_T\) and \(V_{\rm out}\ge v\),

\[
\boxed{V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-A(V_{\rm in}-V_T)^2}.
\]

The boundary between saturation and triode occurs at \(V_{\rm out}=v\), giving

\[
A v_b^2+v_b-V_{DD}=0,
\qquad
v_b=\frac{\sqrt{1+4AV_{DD}}-1}{2A},
\]

so \(V_{\rm in,b}=V_T+v_b\).

### Stack in triode

For larger \(V_{\rm in}\),

\[
A(2vD-D^2)=V_{DD}-D,
\]

or

\[
AD^2-(1+2Av)D+V_{DD}=0.
\]

The physical root is

\[
\boxed{
V_{\rm out}=
\frac{1+2Av-\sqrt{(1+2Av)^2-4AV_{DD}}}{2A}
}.
\]

Thus \(V_{OH}=V_{DD}\), and in the ideal model \(V_{\rm out}\rightarrow0\) as \(V_{\rm in}\rightarrow\infty\).

---

## 3. Small-signal gain

In the stack-saturation region,

\[
g_{m,\rm eq}=\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{\rm in}}
            =\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{\rm in}-V_T)
            =\beta_{\rm eq}v.
\]

With \(\lambda=0\), the stack has infinite output resistance, so

\[
\boxed{
A_v=-g_{m,\rm eq}R_D
=-\frac{\beta R_D}{2}(V_{\rm in}-V_T)
}.
\]

The transconductance is half that of one \(L\)-long transistor at the same gate overdrive, as expected for an effective \(2L\) device. With finite output resistance,

\[
A_v\simeq-g_{m,\rm eq}(R_D\parallel r_{o,\rm stack}).
\]

---

## 4. Why it behaves like an “effective long-channel” device

Include channel-length modulation with coefficient \(\lambda\) for each \(L\)-long transistor. The floating intermediate node provides source feedback: when \(V_{\rm out}\) rises, \(V_X\) rises, reducing \(V_{GS2}\) and opposing the increase in current caused by channel-length modulation.

At low frequency,

\[
r_{o,\rm stack}
=
\frac{g_{d1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2}}
     {g_{d1}g_{o2}},
\]

where \(g_{d1}\) is the triode-region drain conductance of \(M_1\), and \(g_{o2}\) is the output conductance of \(M_2\). For equal devices, no body effect, and \(g_{o2}\ll g_{m2}\),

\[
g_{d1}\simeq g_{m2}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
r_{o,\rm stack}\simeq \frac{2}{g_{o2}}.
\]

Equivalently, to first order in \(\lambda\),

\[
I_D\simeq \frac{\beta v^2}{4}
\left(1+\frac{\lambda}{2}V_{\rm out}\right),
\]

so

\[
\boxed{\lambda_{\rm eq}\simeq\frac{\lambda}{2}},\qquad
\boxed{V_{A,\rm eq}\simeq2V_A}.
\]

A physical \(2L\) transistor likewise has half the \(\beta\) and approximately half the channel-length-modulation coefficient. This is why the tied-gate stack is often called a **self-cascode** or an effective long-channel transistor: it has lower current and transconductance but larger output resistance and intrinsic gain. For \(N\) equal devices, the first-order result is \(\beta_{\rm eq}\approx\beta/N\) and \(\lambda_{\rm eq}\approx\lambda/N\).

---

## 5. Practical limitations

For a common-substrate IC implementation, \(M_2\) has \(V_{SB}=V_X>0\), so

\[
V_{T2}=V_{T0}+\gamma
\left(\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_X}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}\right).
\]

This body effect reduces the stack current, so the exact \(\beta/2\), \(2L\) equivalence is lost. Defining \(\Delta V_T(V_X)=V_{T2}-V_{T0}\), the saturation-region equations become

\[
\frac{\beta}{2}\left[v^2-(v-V_X)^2\right]
=
\frac{\beta}{2}\left[v-V_X-\Delta V_T(V_X)\right]^2,
\]

which generally must be solved numerically together with the load line. Body-effect transconductance \(g_{mb2}\) provides additional source feedback and usually increases the output resistance further.

Parasitic capacitance at \(V_X\), velocity saturation, and DIBL also make the equivalence mainly a dc/low-frequency approximation. If each body can be tied to its own source, or body effect is neglected, the ideal \(2L\)-equivalence above is exact.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate-drive series pair and derives the effective channel length as 2L (and the unequal-device relation). However, it also labels the stack a “self-cascode,” contrary to the golden solution’s caveat against cascode classification.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
Let \(V_X\) be the intermediate node between \(M_1\) and \(M_2\). Assume initially that the two NMOS devices are identical, with

\[
k_n=\mu_n C_{\rm ox}\frac WL,\qquad \lambda=0,\qquad \gamma=0,
\]

and define the overdrive

\[
A=V_{\rm in}-V_T .
\]

## 1. Equivalent transistor of the series pair

For \(A>0\), \(M_1\) has \(V_{GS1}=V_{\rm in}\) and \(V_{DS1}=V_X\). In triode,

\[
I_1=k_n\left(A V_X-\frac{V_X^2}{2}\right)
   =\frac{k_n}{2}\left[A^2-(A-V_X)^2\right].
\]

For \(M_2\), \(V_{GS2}=V_{\rm in}-V_X\) and \(V_{DS2}=V_{\rm out}-V_X\). In triode,

\[
I_2=k_n\left[(A-V_X)(V_{\rm out}-V_X)
-\frac{(V_{\rm out}-V_X)^2}{2}\right]
\]

or

\[
I_2=\frac{k_n}{2}\left[(A-V_X)^2-(A-V_{\rm out})^2\right].
\]

Since \(I_1=I_2\equiv I_D\),

\[
A^2-(A-V_X)^2=(A-V_X)^2-(A-V_{\rm out})^2,
\]

and hence

\[
I_D=\frac{k_n}{4}\left[A^2-(A-V_{\rm out})^2\right]
   =\frac{k_n}{4}\left(2A V_{\rm out}-V_{\rm out}^2\right).
\]

This is exactly the triode current of one NMOS with

\[
\boxed{\left(\frac WL\right)_{\rm eff}=\frac{W}{2L}},\qquad
\boxed{k_{\rm eff}=\frac{k_n}{2}},
\]

and threshold \(V_T\). Therefore the stack is equivalent to a transistor having twice the channel length:

\[
I_D=
\begin{cases}
0, & V_{\rm in}\le V_T,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{k_n}{2}
\left[A V_{\rm out}-\dfrac{V_{\rm out}^2}{2}\right],
& 0<V_{\rm out}<A,\\[10pt]
\dfrac{k_n}{4}A^2,
& V_{\rm out}\ge A .
\end{cases}
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{I_{D,\rm sat}=\frac14\mu_nC_{\rm ox}\frac WL(V_{\rm in}-V_T)^2}
\]

which is one-half the saturation current of either individual transistor. In deep triode, \(R_{\rm on}\) is approximately doubled.

The effective threshold is still \(V_T\), not \(2V_T\): at the onset of conduction no current flows, so \(V_X\simeq0\) and both devices have \(V_{GS}=V_{\rm in}\).

### Internal-node voltage

In the triode region,

\[
\boxed{
V_X=A-\sqrt{\frac{A^2+(A-V_{\rm out})^2}{2}}
}.
\]

When the stack is saturated, \(M_2\) saturates while \(M_1\) remains in triode:

\[
\boxed{V_X=A\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)},\qquad
\boxed{I_D=\frac{k_nA^2}{4}}.
\]

The saturation condition is

\[
V_{\rm out}\ge A=V_{\rm in}-V_T.
\]

A useful generalization is that \(N\) identical series devices with tied gates behave, in the ideal long-channel model, like one device with \(L_{\rm eff}=NL\), \(k_{\rm eff}=k_n/N\).

---

## 2. DC transfer characteristic with \(R_D\)

The resistor imposes the load line

\[
I_D=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}}{R_D}.
\]

Let

\[
\alpha=k_{\rm eff}R_D=\frac{k_nR_D}{2}.
\]

The transition from saturation to triode occurs when \(V_{\rm out}=A\), giving

\[
\boxed{
A_b=\frac{\sqrt{1+2\alpha V_{DD}}-1}{\alpha}
},\qquad
V_{\rm in,b}=V_T+A_b .
\]

The complete output characteristic is therefore

\[
V_{\rm out}=
\begin{cases}
V_{DD}, & A\le 0,\\[5pt]
V_{DD}-\dfrac{\alpha}{2}A^2,
& 0<A\le A_b,\\[10pt]
A+\dfrac1\alpha-
\sqrt{\left(A+\dfrac1\alpha\right)^2-\dfrac{2V_{DD}}{\alpha}},
& A>A_b .
\end{cases}
\]

For small \(V_{\rm in}\), both devices are off. Just above \(V_T\), \(M_2\) is saturated and \(M_1\) is in triode. For sufficiently large \(V_{\rm in}\), both are in triode and \(V_{\rm out}\to0\).

---

## 3. Small-signal behavior

For \(V_{\rm in}\) as the signal and \(V_{DD}\) as AC ground:

- In stack saturation,

\[
\boxed{g_{m,\rm eff}=k_{\rm eff}A=\frac{k_n}{2}(V_{\rm in}-V_T)}
\]

and, with \(\lambda=0\),

\[
\boxed{\frac{dV_{\rm out}}{dV_{\rm in}}
=-g_{m,\rm eff}R_D } .
\]

- In triode,

\[
g_m=k_{\rm eff}V_{\rm out},\qquad
g_{ds}=k_{\rm eff}(A-V_{\rm out}),
\]

so

\[
\frac{dV_{\rm out}}{dV_{\rm in}}
=-\frac{g_mR_D}{1+g_{ds}R_D}.
\]

If channel-length modulation is included and \(\lambda\propto1/L\), the ideal \(2L\) equivalent has approximately \(\lambda_{\rm eff}\simeq\lambda/2\), or \(r_{o,\rm stack}\simeq2/(\lambda I_D)\).

---

## 4. Body effect and short-channel limitations

If both bodies are at ground, the upper transistor has \(V_{SB2}=V_X\), so

\[
V_{T2}=V_{T0}+\Delta(V_X),\qquad
\Delta(V_X)=\gamma\!\left[\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_X}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}\right].
\]

With the usual source-referenced square-law model, the saturation equations become

\[
I_D=\frac{k_n}{2}\left[A^2-(A-V_X)^2\right]
\]

for \(M_1\), and

\[
I_D=\frac{k_n}{2}\left[A-V_X-\Delta(V_X)\right]^2
\]

for \(M_2\). These must be solved implicitly. Body effect raises \(M_2\)'s threshold, reduces the current, and makes the simple constant-threshold \(W/(2L)\) equivalent inexact.

For a charge-sheet long-channel model in which threshold is evaluated at the local channel voltage, the two channels still add to one continuous \(2L\) channel, but with a body-effect-modified \(I\)-\(V\) law. Velocity saturation, DIBL, mobility degradation, and resistance of the intermediate diffusion also invalidate the exact \(L_{\rm eff}=2L\) scaling; the individual device equations must then be solved.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate series NMOS stack and concludes that equal devices behave approximately like a device with twice the channel length. The additional analysis is not needed for full credit.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
## Assumptions

Let \(V_X\) be the node between \(M_1\) and \(M_2\). Assume initially that the two devices are identical, with

\[
\beta=\mu_n C'_{\rm ox}\frac WL ,
\]

common threshold \(V_{TN}\), and ideal long-channel square-law behavior with \(\lambda=\gamma=0\). Thus, for one device,

\[
I_D=
\begin{cases}
\beta\left[(V_{GS}-V_{TN})V_{DS}-\dfrac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right],&\text{triode},\\[2mm]
\dfrac{\beta}{2}(V_{GS}-V_{TN})^2,&\text{saturation}.
\end{cases}
\]

Define the gate overdrive relative to ground as

\[
A=V_{\rm in}-V_{TN},\qquad V\equiv V_{\rm out}.
\]

---

## 1. Operating regions

For \(A\le 0\), both devices are off:

\[
I_D=0,\qquad V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}.
\]

For \(A>0\), \(M_1\) cannot be saturated with nonzero current:

- \(M_1\) saturation requires \(V_X\ge A\).
- \(M_2\) conduction requires \(V_{GS2}=V_{\rm in}-V_X>V_{TN}\), i.e. \(V_X<A\).

Hence \(M_1\) is always in triode. The upper device \(M_2\) is saturated when

\[
V_{\rm out}-V_X \ge V_{\rm in}-V_X-V_{TN}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
V_{\rm out}\ge A .
\]

Otherwise it is in triode.

---

## 2. Current through the series stack

For operation in triode, it is useful to write the current in endpoint form:

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}
\left[(V_G-V_{TN}-V_s)^2-(V_G-V_{TN}-V_d)^2\right].
\]

Thus

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}\left[A^2-(A-V_X)^2\right] \qquad (M_1),
\]

and, when \(M_2\) is in triode,

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}\left[(A-V_X)^2-(A-V)^2\right] \qquad (M_2).
\]

Equating these currents gives

\[
(A-V_X)^2=\frac{A^2+(A-V)^2}{2},
\]

and therefore

\[
\boxed{
I_D=\frac{\beta}{4}\left[A^2-(A-V)^2\right]
=\frac{\beta}{2}\left(AV-\frac{V^2}{2}\right)
}
\]

for \(0\le V<A\). The internal-node voltage is

\[
\boxed{
V_X=A-\sqrt{\frac{A^2+(A-V)^2}{2}}
}.
\]

When \(M_2\) saturates, \(V\ge A\). Equating \(M_1\)'s triode current with \(M_2\)'s saturation current,

\[
\frac{\beta}{2}\left[A^2-(A-V_X)^2\right]
=\frac{\beta}{2}(A-V_X)^2,
\]

gives

\[
V_X=A\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right),
\qquad
\boxed{I_{D,\rm sat}=\frac{\beta}{4}A^2}.
\]

Consequently, the complete stack characteristic is

\[
\boxed{
I_D=
\begin{cases}
0, & A\le0,\\[1mm]
\dfrac{\beta}{4}A^2, & A>0,\; V\ge A,\\[2mm]
\dfrac{\beta}{2}\left(AV-\dfrac{V^2}{2}\right),
& A>0,\;0\le V<A.
\end{cases}}
\]

---

## 3. Equivalent long-channel transistor

Define

\[
\beta_{\rm eq}=\frac{\beta}{2}.
\]

Then

\[
I_D=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\beta_{\rm eq}}{2}A^2,& V\ge A,\\[2mm]
\beta_{\rm eq}\left(AV-\dfrac{V^2}{2}\right),& V<A,
\end{cases}
\]

which is exactly the square-law characteristic of one NMOS with

\[
\boxed{\beta_{\rm eq}=\frac{\beta}{2}},\qquad
\boxed{\left(\frac WL\right)_{\rm eq}=\frac12\frac WL}.
\]

For equal width and process parameters,

\[
\boxed{L_{\rm eq}=2L}.
\]

Thus the two-transistor stack behaves externally as a single NMOS of twice the channel length, with the same threshold voltage. For \(N\) identical devices,

\[
\beta_{\rm eq}=\frac{\beta}{N},\qquad L_{\rm eq}=NL.
\]

More generally, for unequal devices,

\[
\boxed{\frac1{\beta_{\rm eq}}=
\frac1{\beta_1}+\frac1{\beta_2}+\cdots},
\]

so for equal widths and mobility, \(L_{\rm eq}=\sum_i L_i\).

---

## 4. DC transfer characteristic with \(R_D\)

The resistor imposes

\[
V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-R_D I_D.
\]

### Upper transistor saturated

For \(V_{\rm out}\ge A\),

\[
\boxed{
V_{\rm out}=V_{DD}-\frac{R_D\beta}{4}
(V_{\rm in}-V_{TN})^2
=
V_{DD}-\frac{R_D\beta_{\rm eq}}{2}A^2
}.
\]

The boundary between saturation and triode operation occurs when \(V_{\rm out}=A\). If \(A_B=V_{\rm in,B}-V_{TN}\),

\[
\boxed{
A_B=
\frac{\sqrt{1+2R_D\beta_{\rm eq}V_{DD}}-1}
{R_D\beta_{\rm eq}}
=
\frac{2\left[\sqrt{1+R_D\beta V_{DD}}-1\right]}
{R_D\beta}
}.
\]

### Both devices in triode

For \(A>A_B\),

\[
\boxed{
V_{DD}-V_{\rm out}
=R_D\beta_{\rm eq}
\left(A V_{\rm out}-\frac{V_{\rm out}^2}{2}\right)
}.
\]

The physical low-output root is

\[
\boxed{
V_{\rm out}=
\frac{1+pA-\sqrt{(1+pA)^2-2pV_{DD}}}{p},
\qquad p=R_D\beta_{\rm eq}.
}
\]

The logic-high output is \(V_{OH}=V_{DD}\); \(V_{OL}\) is found by setting \(A=V_{DD}-V_{TN}\) in the triode expression.

The switching threshold \(V_M\), defined by \(V_{\rm in}=V_{\rm out}=V_M\), lies in the saturation branch:

\[
\boxed{
V_M=V_{TN}+
\frac{\sqrt{1+2R_D\beta_{\rm eq}(V_{DD}-V_{TN})}-1}
{R_D\beta_{\rm eq}}
}.
\]

---

## 5. Small-signal behavior

In the saturation/high-gain region,

\[
\boxed{g_{m,\rm eq}=\beta_{\rm eq}A
=\frac{\beta}{2}(V_{\rm in}-V_{TN})}.
\]

With \(\lambda=0\),

\[
\boxed{A_v\simeq-g_{m,\rm eq}R_D}.
\]

In the triode region,

\[
g_m=\beta_{\rm eq}V_{\rm out},\qquad
g_{ds}=\beta_{\rm eq}(A-V_{\rm out}),
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
A_v=-\frac{g_m}{1/R_D+g_{ds}}
}.
\]

If channel-length modulation is retained, the approximately equivalent \(2L\) device has \(\lambda_{\rm eq}\simeq\lambda/2\), so

\[
A_v\simeq-g_{m,\rm eq}(R_D\parallel r_{o,\rm eq}).
\]

---

## 6. Body effect and other nonidealities

In a common substrate, \(M_2\) has \(V_{SB2}=V_X>0\), so

\[
V_{T2}=V_{T0}+
\gamma\left(\sqrt{2\phi_F+V_X}-\sqrt{2\phi_F}\right).
\]

This raises \(M_2\)'s threshold and reduces the current below the ideal value \(\beta A^2/4\). For example, in saturation, with  
\(\Delta V_T=\Delta V_T(V_X)\),

\[
I_D=\frac{\beta}{2}\left[A^2-(A-V_X)^2\right]
=\frac{\beta}{2}\left[A-V_X-\Delta V_T\right]^2,
\]

which must be solved implicitly for \(V_X\). Saturation then begins at

\[
V_{\rm out}\ge A-\Delta V_T(V_X).
\]

Therefore the exact \(L_{\rm eq}=2L\) result requires negligible body effect, or each device body tied to its own source. Channel-length modulation, velocity saturation, mobility degradation, and short-channel effects also make the equivalence approximate.

**Main result:** under the ideal long-channel square-law model, the stack is equivalent to one NMOS with twice the channel length, half the transconductance parameter, and half the current of a single \(W/L\) device at the same gate overdrive.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate series NMOS stack and concludes that its effective channel length is approximately the sum of the device lengths. The equal-device result, β_eq = β/2 and L_eq = 2L, matches the golden solution.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
Let \(X\) denote the common source/tail node and \(I_T=I_1\). Assume both MOSFETs are in saturation and \(I_1\) is an ideal dc current source, hence an open circuit for small signals. Also, \(V_{DD}\) and \(V_b\) are ac ground.

## DC operation

KCL at \(X\) gives

\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_T,
\qquad
V_{\text{out},Q}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D .
\]

For identical devices and a balanced bias \(V_{in,Q}=V_b\),

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_T}{2},
\qquad
V_{\text{out},Q}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_T R_D}{2}.
\]

The circuit is a differential pair in disguise: its left drain is simply connected to \(V_{DD}\), and the output is taken from the right drain.

---

## Small-signal voltage gain

The source follower \(M_1\) sees the low resistance looking into the source of the common-gate device \(M_2\); thus its gain is not approximately unity.

Neglecting body effect and channel-length modulation,

\[
i_{d1}=g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_x),\qquad
i_{d2}=-g_{m2}v_x .
\]

Because the ideal tail source has zero incremental current,

\[
i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0,
\]

so

\[
\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}
  =\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}.
\]

At the output,

\[
v_{\text{out}}=-R_D i_{d2}=g_{m2}R_Dv_x.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
A_v\equiv\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{in}}
 =\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D
}
\]

and the gain is positive. An increase in \(V_{in}\) steers current from \(M_2\) to \(M_1\), reducing the drop across \(R_D\) and raising \(V_{\text{out}}\).

For identical devices at the balanced point, \(g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m\):

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}=\frac12,\qquad
A_v=+\frac{g_mR_D}{2}}.
\]

If \(V_b\) also carries a small signal,

\[
v_{\text{out}}\simeq \frac{g_mR_D}{2}(v_{in}-v_b).
\]

With \(\beta=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)\), the balanced-bias transconductance is

\[
g_m=\sqrt{\beta I_T},
\]

so \(A_v=(R_D/2)\sqrt{\beta I_T}\).

### Including body effect

Let \(g_{mbi}\) be the body-effect transconductance. Then

\[
\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}
=\frac{g_{m1}}
 {g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}},
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
A_v=
\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})}
 {g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}R_D
}.
\]

For matched devices, \(g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m\) and \(g_{mb1}=g_{mb2}=g_{mb}\), giving again

\[
\boxed{A_v=\frac{g_mR_D}{2}}.
\]

Thus body effect changes the source-node gain \(v_x/v_{in}\), but cancels from the overall gain of the matched pair.

---

## Finite transistor output resistance

For an ideal tail source, define

\[
G_i=g_{mi}+g_{mbi}+g_{oi},\qquad
G_D=\frac1{R_D},
\]

where \(g_{oi}=1/r_{oi}\). The general gain is

\[
\boxed{
A_v=
\frac{g_{m1}G_2}
{(G_D+g_{o2})G_1+G_2G_D}
}.
\]

For matched devices with \(r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_o\),

\[
A_v
=\frac{g_m}{2/R_D+1/r_o}
=\frac{g_mR_D}{2+R_D/r_o}
=\boxed{\frac{g_m}{2}\left(R_D\parallel 2r_o\right)}.
\]

This reduces to \(g_mR_D/2\) for \(r_o\to\infty\).

---

## Impedances and operating limits

- Low-frequency input resistance: \(R_{in}\to\infty\), since the input is an MOS gate.
- With \(\lambda=0\): \(\;R_{\text{out}}\simeq R_D\).
- With matched finite-\(r_o\) devices and an ideal tail source:
  \[
  \boxed{R_{\text{out}}\simeq R_D\parallel 2r_o}.
  \]
- Current-steering extremes, subject to saturation and current-source compliance:
  \[
  V_{in}\gg V_b:\ I_{D2}\to0,\quad V_{\text{out}}\to V_{DD},
  \]
  \[
  V_{in}\ll V_b:\ I_{D2}\to I_T,\quad V_{\text{out}}\to V_{DD}-I_TR_D.
  \]
- Saturation requires approximately
  \[
  V_{DD}-V_X\ge V_{OV1},\qquad
  V_{\text{out}}-V_X\ge V_{OV2},
  \]
  together with sufficient voltage across \(I_1\).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-follower M1 driving the common-gate M2 and derives the positive gain and key loading effects consistently. The differential-pair analogy is compatible with this topology; the additional small-signal and impedance analysis is sound under its stated assumptions.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
The circuit is both a **source-follower/common-gate cascade** and, equivalently, one half of an NMOS differential pair: \(M_1\) is a source follower, \(M_2\) is common-gate, and the ideal current sink forces their total current to remain constant.

Let \(v_x\) be the small-signal voltage at the common source node. \(V_{DD}\), \(V_b\), and the ideal current source are ac ground/open, respectively.

## DC operation

\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_1,\qquad V_{\text{out}}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D.
\]

For identical devices biased at \(V_{in,Q}=V_b\),

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_1}{2},\qquad
V_{\text{out},Q}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_1R_D}{2}.
\]

A positive \(v_{in}\) steers tail current from \(M_2\) toward \(M_1\), reducing \(I_{D2}\), reducing the drop across \(R_D\), and therefore raising \(v_{\text{out}}\). Thus the gain is noninverting.

---

## Small-signal gain, ideal MOS model

First neglect channel-length modulation. Define, including body effect,

\[
G_1=g_{m1}+g_{mb1},\qquad G_2=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}.
\]

With \(v_b=0\), the incremental drain currents into the common source node are

\[
i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}-G_1v_x,
\qquad
i_{d2}=-G_2v_x .
\]

Since the ideal tail source has zero incremental current,

\[
i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
v_x=\frac{g_{m1}}{G_1+G_2}\,v_{in}.
\]

At the output,

\[
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{R_D}+i_{d2}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
v_{\text{out}}=G_2R_Dv_x.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{v_{in}}
=\frac{g_{m1}G_2}{G_1+G_2}R_D
}
\]

or, if body effect is neglected,

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D
}.
\]

This can be viewed as

\[
A_{\text{SF}}=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}},
\qquad
A_{\text{CG}}=g_{m2}R_D.
\]

For matched transistors, \(g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m\),

\[
\boxed{A_v=+\frac{g_mR_D}{2}}.
\]

Including body effect for matched devices gives the same result:

\[
A_{\text{SF}}=\frac{g_m}{2(g_m+g_{mb})},\qquad
A_{\text{CG}}=(g_m+g_{mb})R_D,
\]

so the body-effect factors cancel. More generally, if \(V_b\) also carries a signal,

\[
v_{\text{out}}
=\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D\,(v_{in}-v_b),
\]

showing the differential-pair nature of the circuit.

### Impedances

- Input resistance at \(V_{in}\): \(R_{in}\to\infty\) at low frequency, since it is a MOS gate.
- Input resistance looking into the source of \(M_2\):
  \[
  R_{in,\text{CG}}\simeq \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}.
  \]
- With \(\lambda=0\): \(R_{\text{out}}=R_D\).

---

## Including finite transistor output resistance

For a complete low-frequency result, let

\[
g_{oj}=\frac{1}{r_{oj}},\qquad
g_t=\frac{1}{r_t},\qquad
G_D=\frac{1}{R_D},
\]

where \(r_t\) is the output resistance of the tail current source (\(g_t=0\) for ideal \(I_1\)), and define

\[
S=G_1+G_2+g_{o1}+g_{o2}+g_t.
\]

The transistor network seen at the output has the Norton equivalent

\[
G_{m,\text{eff}}
=\frac{g_{m1}(G_2+g_{o2})}{S},
\]

\[
r_{o,\text{eff}}
=\frac{S}{g_{o2}(G_1+g_{o1}+g_t)}.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
A_v=
G_{m,\text{eff}}\left(R_D\parallel r_{o,\text{eff}}\right)
=
\frac{g_{m1}(G_2+g_{o2})}
{G_DS+g_{o2}(G_1+g_{o1}+g_t)}
}
\]

and

\[
R_{\text{out}}=R_D\parallel r_{o,\text{eff}}.
\]

For matched devices, an ideal tail source, and \(r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_o\), this simplifies exactly to

\[
G_{m,\text{eff}}=\frac{g_m}{2},\qquad
r_{o,\text{eff}}=2r_o,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{
A_v=\frac{g_m}{2}\left(R_D\parallel 2r_o\right),
\qquad
R_{\text{out}}=R_D\parallel 2r_o
}.
\]

Taking \(r_o\to\infty\) recovers \(A_v=g_mR_D/2\) and \(R_{\text{out}}=R_D\).

---

## Large-signal/headroom notes

For identical square-law devices with \(I_D=(\beta/2)V_{OV}^2\), \(\Delta V=V_{in}-V_b\), and both devices conducting,

\[
I_{D2}
=
\frac{I_1}{2}
-\frac{\beta\Delta V}{4}
\sqrt{\frac{4I_1}{\beta}-\Delta V^2},
\qquad
V_{\text{out}}=V_{DD}-R_DI_{D2}.
\]

For sufficiently positive \(\Delta V\), \(M_2\) turns off and \(V_{\text{out}}\to V_{DD}\); for sufficiently negative \(\Delta V\), \(M_2\) carries all of \(I_1\) and \(V_{\text{out}}\to V_{DD}-I_1R_D\), subject to saturation and current-source compliance. In particular,

\[
V_{\text{out}}\gtrsim V_b-V_T
\]

is required to keep \(M_2\) in saturation, and the common-source node must remain above the minimum compliance voltage of \(I_1\).

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as a source follower driving M2 in common-gate, with the intermediate source node conveying the signal to the loaded output. The current-steering and noninverting-gain analysis is consistent with that topology; the extra detail does not undermine the central answer.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
Let \(v_x\) denote the common-source node. The supplies and the bias \(V_b\) are small-signal grounds. The circuit is essentially a differential pair with only the drain of \(M_2\) used as an output: \(M_1\) is a source follower driving the source terminal of the common-gate device \(M_2\).

## 1. DC operation

The tail source imposes

\[
I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_1,
\qquad
V_{OQ}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D .
\]

For identical transistors and \(V_{in,Q}=V_b\),

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_1}{2},
\]

\[
V_X=V_b-V_{GS},
\qquad
V_{OQ}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_1R_D}{2}.
\]

For square-law devices with \(k=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)\),

\[
g_m=\sqrt{kI_1}
\]

for each transistor at this bias point. The devices must remain saturated; in particular, approximately \(V_{\text{out}}\ge V_b-V_{TH}\), and the tail source must have enough voltage compliance.

---

## 2. Small-signal voltage gain

First neglect channel-length modulation, body effect, and the output resistance of \(I_1\). Then

\[
i_{d1}=g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_x),\qquad
i_{d2}=g_{m2}(v_b-v_x).
\]

Since the tail current is constant,

\[
i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0.
\]

With \(v_b=0\) in small signal,

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}}.
\]

Thus the source follower is loaded by the common-gate input resistance of \(M_2\), approximately \(1/g_{m2}\); it does not have unity gain.

The incremental drain current of \(M_2\) is

\[
i_{d2}=-g_{m2}v_x,
\]

and

\[
v_{out}=-R_D i_{d2}=g_{m2}R_Dv_x.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D
}
\]

or, for matched devices \(g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m\),

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}=\frac12,\qquad
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=+\frac{g_mR_D}{2}}.
\]

The gain is positive: a positive \(v_{in}\) raises \(v_x\), increasing \(I_{D1}\) and decreasing \(I_{D2}\). The smaller voltage drop across \(R_D\) makes \(v_{out}\) rise.

More generally, if \(V_b\) also has a small-signal component,

\[
\boxed{
v_{out}
=
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D
\left(v_{in}-v_b\right)
}
\]

so the circuit is a single-ended differential amplifier. With an ideal tail source its common-mode gain is zero. Any load \(R_L\) replaces \(R_D\) by \(R_D\parallel R_L\).

---

## 3. Nonideal effects

### Finite tail-source resistance

If \(I_1\) has output resistance \(r_t\), with \(\lambda=\gamma=0\),

\[
A_v=
R_D\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}
{g_{m1}+g_{m2}+1/r_t}.
\]

For matched transistors,

\[
A_v=
\frac{g_mR_D/2}
{1+1/(2g_mr_t)}.
\]

### Body effect

With body effect but negligible \(r_o\) and an ideal tail source,

\[
A_v=
R_D\,
\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})}
{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}.
\]

For matched transistors, or when \(g_{mb}/g_m\) is the same for both devices, the body-effect terms cancel and the result remains \(g_mR_D/2\).

### Channel-length modulation

For identical devices with \(r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_o\), ideal tail current, and including body effect,

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{out}}=R_D\parallel 2r_o}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
A_v=+\frac{g_m}{2}\left(R_D\parallel 2r_o\right)
}.
\]

When \(r_o\to\infty\), these reduce to \(R_{\text{out}}=R_D\) and \(A_v=g_mR_D/2\).

A completely general low-frequency result can be obtained by defining

\[
a_1=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1},\quad
b_2=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o2},\quad
s=a_1+b_2+g_t,
\]

where \(g_{oi}=1/r_{oi}\), \(g_t=1/r_t\), and \(g_D=1/R_D\). Then

\[
\boxed{
A_v=
\frac{g_{m1}b_2}
{g_Ds+g_{o2}(a_1+g_t)}
},
\qquad
\boxed{
R_{\text{out}}
=
\left[g_D+
\frac{g_{o2}(a_1+g_t)}{s}
\right]^{-1}.
}
\]

---

## 4. Terminal behavior and swing

- Low-frequency input resistance is ideally infinite because the input is a MOS gate.
- Output resistance is approximately \(R_D\) when \(r_o\) is neglected, or \(R_D\parallel2r_o\) for matched finite-\(r_o\) devices.
- Since \(v_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_D\), steering all \(I_1\) into \(M_2\) gives the lowest ideal output \(V_{DD}-I_1R_D\), while turning \(M_2\) off gives \(V_{DD}\). Practical limits are set by saturation and tail-current-source compliance.

The small-signal signal path, gain direction, and principal idealized gain are consistent with that topology; the added details do not undermine the essential analysis.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
The inductive behavior is a **small-signal, frequency-dependent effect** caused mainly by the finite source resistance \(R_S\) driving the gate of \(M_1\), together with \(M_1\)’s gate-source capacitance \(C_{GS}\).

To find \(Z_{\text{out}}\), set the independent sources to zero: \(V_{in}=0\), \(V_{DD}\) is ac ground, and \(V_b\) is ac ground. Thus the gate of \(M_1\) is connected to ground through \(R_S\). Let \(v_x\) be a test voltage applied at \(V_{\text{out}}\), and let \(v_g\) be the small-signal gate voltage of \(M_1\). Ignoring other capacitances for clarity, with \(C=C_{GS1}\),

\[
\frac{v_g}{R_S}+sC(v_g-v_x)=0
\]

so

\[
v_g=\frac{sR_SC}{1+sR_SC}v_x .
\]

The current drawn from the output node into \(M_1\) is approximately

\[
i_x=(g_m+sC)(v_x-v_g)
     =\frac{g_m+sC}{1+sR_SC}v_x .
\]

Thus the active part of the output impedance is

\[
Z_{\text{out},M1}
=\frac{v_x}{i_x}
=\frac{1+sR_SC}{g_m+sC}
=\frac{1}{g_m}\frac{1+sR_SC}{1+sC/g_m}.
\]

This impedance has a zero at

\[
\omega_z=\frac{1}{R_SC}
\]

and a pole at

\[
\omega_p=\frac{g_m}{C}.
\]

If

\[
R_S>\frac{1}{g_m},
\]

then \(\omega_z<\omega_p\). In that frequency range, \(|Z_{\text{out}}|\) increases with frequency and the phase of \(Z_{\text{out}}\) is positive: voltage leads current. That is inductive behavior. For low frequencies,

\[
Z_{\text{out},M1}
\approx \frac{1}{g_m}
+s\left[\frac{C}{g_m}\left(R_S-\frac{1}{g_m}\right)\right],
\]

so it looks like a resistance \(1/g_m\) in series with an inductance

\[
L_{\text{eq}}
=\frac{C}{g_m}\left(R_S-\frac{1}{g_m}\right)>0 .
\]

Physically: at low frequency the gate is held near ac ground through \(R_S\), so the source follower has low output resistance \(\approx 1/g_m\). At higher frequency, \(C_{GS}\) couples the output/source motion back to the gate; the gate partially follows the source, reducing \(v_{GS}\) and reducing the \(g_m\) feedback current. Since the gate voltage can only follow through the finite \(R_S C_{GS}\) network, the current response lags the applied voltage, giving an inductive impedance.

\(M_2\) mainly provides bias current; its small-signal \(g_m\) is zero because its gate is ac grounded. Its \(r_o\) and output capacitances simply shunt the output. Those parasitics can reduce or cancel the inductive effect. Including a direct output capacitance \(C_o\), the low-frequency effective inductance is positive only if roughly

\[
C_{GS}(g_mR_S-1)>C_o .
\]

So the circuit does not contain a physical inductor; it synthesizes an inductive output impedance over a finite frequency range, provided the source resistance is sufficiently large.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the C_GS1–R_S transition, derives the low- and high-frequency limits (1/g_m1 and R_S), and explains when the impedance has positive phase and appears inductive. The parasitic-loading caveat is also appropriate.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
It is a **small-signal active-inductor effect** caused mainly by the finite source resistance \(R_S\) and the gate-source capacitance \(C_{GS}\) of \(M_1\). There is no physical inductor in the circuit.

To see this, set \(V_{in}=0\) for the output-impedance calculation, so \(V_{DD}\), \(V_b\), and the left side of \(R_S\) are ac grounds. Apply a test voltage \(v_x\) at \(V_{out}\). Neglecting less important parasitics first, the gate node of \(M_1\) satisfies

\[
\frac{v_g}{R_S}+sC_{GS}(v_g-v_x)=0
\]

so

\[
\frac{v_g}{v_x}=\frac{sR_S C_{GS}}{1+sR_S C_{GS}}.
\]

At low frequency the gate is approximately grounded; at high frequency \(C_{GS}\) couples the output/source voltage back to the gate, so the gate tends to follow the source. That reduces \(v_{gs}=v_g-v_x\) and weakens the source-follower action that gives a low output resistance.

The current drawn from the test source is approximately

\[
i_x=(g_{m1}+sC_{GS})(v_x-v_g),
\]

hence, ignoring \(r_o\), body effect, and other capacitances,

\[
Y_{out}=\frac{i_x}{v_x}
      =\frac{g_{m1}+sC_{GS}}{1+sR_S C_{GS}},
\]

and therefore

\[
Z_{out}
=\frac{1+sR_S C_{GS}}{g_{m1}+sC_{GS}}
=\frac{1}{g_{m1}}\,
  \frac{1+s/\omega_z}{1+s/\omega_p},
\]

with

\[
\omega_z=\frac{1}{R_S C_{GS}},\qquad
\omega_p=\frac{g_{m1}}{C_{GS}}.
\]

If

\[
R_S>\frac{1}{g_{m1}},
\]

then \(\omega_z<\omega_p\): the zero occurs before the pole. Between those frequencies \(Z_{out}\) has positive phase and its magnitude rises with frequency, which is inductive behavior. Equivalently, for \(s=j\omega\),

\[
\operatorname{Im}\{Z_{out}\}
=
\frac{\omega C_{GS}(g_{m1}R_S-1)}
     {g_{m1}^2+(\omega C_{GS})^2},
\]

which is positive when \(g_{m1}R_S>1\).

Physically: a positive test voltage at the source is coupled through \(C_{GS}\) to the gate with a phase shift set by \(R_S C_{GS}\). The resulting \(g_m v_{gs}\) current is delayed and can dominate the direct capacitive current, so the current drawn from the test source lags the voltage. That is exactly the small-signature of an inductive impedance.

Including \(r_o\), \(g_{mb}\), \(M_2\)’s output resistance, and capacitances from the output node to ground adds shunt terms \(G_0+sC_L\). The low-frequency admittance becomes roughly

\[
Y_{out}\approx (g_{m1}+G_0)
+s\left[C_L+C_{GS}(1-g_{m1}R_S)\right].
\]

If the bracketed susceptance is negative, \(Z_{out}\approx R+sL\), i.e. inductive. Thus the effect appears when \(R_S\) is sufficiently large and the extra output capacitance is not so large that it masks the inductive phase.

The small-signal derivation and stated parasitic limitations are consistent with the golden solution.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
The circuit is a **source follower** biased by \(M_2\). Its output impedance can look inductive because the gate of \(M_1\) is driven through a finite resistance \(R_S\), and \(M_1\) has a gate-source capacitance \(C_{GS}\).

To measure output impedance, set \(V_{in}\), \(V_b\), and \(V_{DD}\) to ac ground and apply a test voltage \(v_x\) at the output. Ignoring \(r_o\), body effect, and output capacitances for the moment:

\[
\frac{v_g}{R_S}+sC_{GS}(v_g-v_x)=0
\]

so

\[
\frac{v_g}{v_x}=\frac{sR_SC_{GS}}{1+sR_SC_{GS}}.
\]

The current drawn from the output by \(M_1\) is approximately

\[
i_x=(g_m+sC_{GS})(v_x-v_g)
     =\frac{g_m+sC_{GS}}{1+sR_SC_{GS}}\,v_x .
\]

Thus

\[
Z_{out}=\frac{v_x}{i_x}
       =\frac{1+sR_SC_{GS}}{g_m+sC_{GS}}
       =\frac{1}{g_m}\,
         \frac{1+sR_SC_{GS}}{1+sC_{GS}/g_m}.
\]

So \(Z_{out}\) has:

\[
\omega_z=\frac{1}{R_SC_{GS}}, \qquad
\omega_p=\frac{g_m}{C_{GS}}.
\]

If \(R_S>1/g_m\), then \(\omega_z<\omega_p\). In that frequency range, the impedance magnitude rises with frequency and its phase is positive, like

\[
Z_{out}\approx R + sL = R+j\omega L.
\]

A low-frequency expansion gives

\[
Z_{out}\approx
\frac{1}{g_m}
+s\,\frac{C_{GS}(g_mR_S-1)}{g_m^2},
\]

so for \(g_mR_S>1\) the coefficient of \(s\) is positive: an effective inductance appears.

Intuitively: at low frequency, \(C_{GS}\) is open and the gate is approximately ac-grounded, so the source follower has low output resistance \(\sim 1/g_m\). At higher frequency, \(C_{GS}\) couples the output back to the gate; because the gate is tied to ground only through \(R_S\), the gate voltage begins to follow the output. That reduces \(v_{GS}\), reduces the current that \(M_1\) draws for a given output voltage, and therefore increases the output impedance with frequency. An impedance increasing with frequency is inductive.

\(M_2\), body effect, \(r_o\), and output capacitances add shunt conductance/capacitance and can reduce or cancel this effect, so the impedance is inductive only over a finite frequency range and only if the \(R_S\)-\(C_{GS}\) feedback is strong enough.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the gate-source-capacitance feedback and derives the transition from low-frequency output resistance near 1/gm to high-frequency resistance near RS. It also correctly explains the positive phase (inductive behavior) when RS exceeds 1/gm.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
## 1. Circuit and feedback topology

The lower transistor is drawn mirrored: \(M_2\) has its **gate at \(V_{\text{out}}\)**, **drain at node \(X\)**, and source at ground. Thus:

\[
X \xrightarrow{M_1} V_{\text{out}},\qquad
V_{\text{out}} \xrightarrow{M_2} X .
\]

Each common-source path is inverting, so the total loop has two inversions and is therefore a **positive-feedback loop**. The output voltage is sampled at the gate of \(M_2\), while the feedback signal is a current summed with \(I_{\text{in}}\) at \(X\). Hence this is a **shunt–shunt, current-in/voltage-out transimpedance circuit**.

Let \(V_{DD}\) be small-signal ground and define

\[
R_Y=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1},\qquad
A_1=g_{m1}R_Y,
\]

and

\[
R_X=\frac{1}{g_{d2}}\simeq r_{o2},
\]

where \(g_{d2}\) is the small-signal drain conductance of \(M_2\) at \(X\). If \(M_2\) is in triode, its channel conductance should be used rather than \(g_{o2}=\lambda I_D\).

---

## 2. Small-signal gain

At the output node,

\[
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{R_Y}+g_{m1}v_X=0
\]

so

\[
v_{\text{out}}=-A_1v_X.
\]

KCL at node \(X\) gives

\[
i_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_X}{R_X}+g_{m2}v_{\text{out}}.
\]

Substituting the output relation,

\[
i_{\text{in}}
=\left(\frac{1}{R_X}-A_1g_{m2}\right)v_X.
\]

Define the positive round-trip loop gain

\[
T=A_1g_{m2}R_X
  =g_{m1}g_{m2}R_YR_X.
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_X}{i_{\text{in}}}
      =\frac{R_X}{1-T}}
\]

and the closed-loop transimpedance is

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=-\frac{A_1R_X}{1-T}
=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}\frac{T}{T-1}}.
\]

If \(r_{o1}\gg R_{D1}\) and \(R_X=r_{o2}\),

\[
\boxed{
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=
-\frac{g_{m1}R_{D1}r_{o2}}
{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}r_{o2}}
}
\]

with

\[
T=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}r_{o2}.
\]

For \(T\gg1\), the formal gain approaches

\[
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}\approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}}.
\]

---

## 3. Input and output impedances

The input resistance seen by the current source is

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{in}}=\frac{R_X}{1-T}}.
\]

With \(i_{\text{in}}=0\), an output test current gives

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{out}}=\frac{R_Y}{1-T}}.
\]

Thus, for \(0<T<1\), positive feedback increases both impedances and increases the magnitude of the transimpedance:

\[
\left|\frac{v_o}{i_{\text{in}}}\right|
=\frac{A_1R_X}{1-T}>A_1R_X.
\]

---

## 4. Stability

The characteristic denominator is \(1-T\), confirming positive feedback.

- \(T<1\): potentially stable linear operation, but gain and sensitivity are increased.
- \(T=1\): infinite small-signal gain, zero-frequency pole, and marginal stability.
- \(T>1\): \(R_{\text{in}}\) and \(R_{\text{out}}\) become negative and the bias point is regenerative/unstable; the circuit latches until transistor nonlinearity or triode operation establishes another operating point.

With total node capacitances \(C_X,C_Y\),

\[
L(s)=\frac{T}{(1+sR_XC_X)(1+sR_YC_Y)}
\]

and

\[
1-L(s)=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
(1+sR_XC_X)(1+sR_YC_Y)-T=0.
\]

For \(T>1\), this has a right-half-plane pole; for \(T=1\), it has a pole at \(s=0\).

---

## 5. DC operating-point equations

Since MOS gates draw no dc current,

\[
I_{D2}=I_{\text{in}},
\qquad
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}.
\]

If both devices are saturated and square-law with \(\lambda=0\),

\[
I_{\text{in}}
=\frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{\text{out}}-V_{TH2})^2,
\]

hence

\[
V_{\text{out}}
=V_{TH2}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}.
\]

However, \(\lambda_2=0\) gives \(g_{d2}=0\), \(R_X\to\infty\), and therefore \(T\to\infty\): that idealized operating point is locally unstable. A finite \(g_{d2}\), arising from channel-length modulation, triode operation, or an added shunt resistance at \(X\), is required for a stable linear transimpedance amplifier.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M2’s gate connection and the resulting positive-feedback path. Its small-signal input conductance, impedance, and transimpedance expressions capture the key negative-conductance mechanism and the possibility of large or negative input resistance; the added stability discussion is consistent with the stated model.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
Assume both devices are NMOSs operating in saturation, with bodies tied to ground, and initially neglect channel-length modulation and body effect. \(M_2\) is drawn mirrored: its gate is connected to \(V_{\text{out}}\), its drain to node \(X\), and its source to ground.

### Feedback polarity

A perturbation \(v_X>0\) increases \(M_1\)'s drain current and lowers \(V_{\text{out}}\). The lower \(V_{\text{out}}\) reduces \(M_2\)'s drain current, leaving more of \(I_{\text{in}}\) to raise \(v_X\). Thus

\[
v_X\uparrow\ \Rightarrow\ v_{\text{out}}\downarrow\ \Rightarrow\ I_{D2}\downarrow\ \Rightarrow\ v_X\uparrow ,
\]

so the two common-source inversions form a **positive-feedback loop**. It is a current-input/voltage-output (shunt-shunt) feedback circuit.

### First-order small-signal analysis

Let lowercase quantities denote increments about the bias point, with \(i_{\text{in}}\) positive into node \(X\). Since \(V_{DD}\) is ac ground,

\[
g_{m1}v_X+\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}=0
\]

and, at node \(X\),

\[
i_{\text{in}}=g_{m2}v_{\text{out}} .
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}}
\]

and

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_X}{i_{\text{in}}}
      =-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}} } .
\]

Hence the resistance looking into node \(X\) is

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{in},X}
      =-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}} } .
\]

The circuit therefore realizes a **negative small-signal resistance**. Equivalently, applying a test voltage \(v_X\) gives

\[
i_X=g_{m2}v_{\text{out}}
   =-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}v_X .
\]

The same result follows from the dc square-law relations:

\[
I_{\text{in}}=\frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{\text{out}}-V_{Tn})^2,
\qquad
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}}}{R_{D1}}
=\frac{\beta_1}{2}(V_X-V_{Tn})^2,
\]

so that

\[
\frac{\partial V_{\text{out}}}{\partial I_{\text{in}}}
=\frac{1}{g_{m2}},\qquad
\frac{\partial V_X}{\partial I_{\text{in}}}
=-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}.
\]

### Including finite output resistances

Let

\[
R_1=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1},\qquad R_2=r_{o2},
\]

for an ideal current source. The two stage gains are

\[
A_1=-g_{m1}R_1,\qquad A_2=-g_{m2}R_2,
\]

giving the positive loop gain

\[
\boxed{T=A_1A_2=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1R_2}.
\]

The general low-frequency results are then

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{in},X}=\frac{R_2}{1-T}},\qquad
\boxed{R_{\text{out}}=\frac{R_1}{1-T}},
\]

and

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=\frac{g_{m1}R_1R_2}{T-1}
=\frac{T}{g_{m2}(T-1)}} .
\]

For \(T\gg1\), these reduce to

\[
R_{\text{in},X}\simeq-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_1},
\qquad
\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}\simeq\frac{1}{g_{m2}}.
\]

At \(T=1\) the closed-loop equations are singular; for \(T>1\) the isolated bias point is regenerative and generally latches or oscillates with parasitic capacitances. The negative resistance can nevertheless be used to cancel a positive loss resistance in an external resonator or oscillator.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
### 1. Circuit topology and feedback polarity

- \(M_1\) is a common-source stage from node \(X\) to \(V_{\text{out}}\), loaded by
  \[
  R_o=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}.
  \]
- \(M_2\) is a mirrored common-source stage: its gate senses \(V_{\text{out}}\), its drain returns to node \(X\), and its source is grounded. Its drain output resistance is denoted \(R_X\simeq r_{o2}\) (more generally, \(R_X=1/g_{d2}\)).
- The input current and the drain current of \(M_2\) are summed in shunt at \(X\). Thus this is a current-input/voltage-output, or transresistance, feedback circuit with shunt mixing and voltage sampling.

The feedback is regenerative. For example,

\[
V_{\text{out}}\uparrow
\;\Rightarrow\; I_{D2}\uparrow
\;\Rightarrow\; V_X\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; I_{D1}\downarrow
\;\Rightarrow\; V_{\text{out}}\uparrow .
\]

The returned change has the same sign as the initiating change, so the loop is positive feedback.

If the loop is broken at the gate of \(M_2\), a test voltage \(v_t\) gives

\[
v_X=-g_{m2}R_Xv_t,\qquad
v_{\rm ret}=-g_{m1}R_ov_X=L v_t,
\]

where the positive-feedback loop-gain magnitude is

\[
\boxed{L=g_{m1}g_{m2}R_oR_X}
\]

with \(R_o=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\) and \(R_X=r_{o2}\) for saturated devices.

---

### 2. Small-signal gain and input impedance

With \(V_{DD}\) at AC ground,

\[
v_{\text{out}}=-g_{m1}R_o v_X,
\]

and KCL at \(X\) gives

\[
i_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_X}{R_X}+g_{m2}v_{\text{out}}
            =\frac{1-L}{R_X}v_X .
\]

Therefore,

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{in}}=\frac{v_X}{i_{\text{in}}}
      =\frac{R_X}{1-L}}
\]

and the closed-loop transresistance is

\[
\boxed{\frac{v_{\text{out}}}{i_{\text{in}}}
=-\frac{g_{m1}R_oR_X}{1-L}
=\frac{1}{g_{m2}}\frac{L}{L-1}} .
\]

The \(1-L\) denominator is characteristic of positive feedback; negative feedback would give \(1+L\).

With the input current source set to zero, an output test voltage gives similarly

\[
\boxed{R_{\text{out}}=\frac{R_o}{1-L}} .
\]

Thus positive feedback raises both input and output resistances, but only while \(L<1\).

---

### 3. Stability

Including the nodal capacitances \(C_X\) and \(C_o\), the natural-response equation is approximately

\[
\left(\frac1{R_X}+sC_X\right)
\left(\frac1{R_o}+sC_o\right)-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0 .
\]

Its constant term is proportional to \(1-L\). Hence:

- \(L<1\): the linear operating point can be stable; \(R_{\text{in}}\), \(R_{\text{out}}\), and gain are enhanced.
- \(L=1\): the DC conductance vanishes; a pole reaches the origin and the impedances become unbounded.
- \(L>1\): \(R_{\text{in}}\) and \(R_{\text{out}}\) are negative and one pole lies in the right half-plane. No stable linear bias exists; the circuit regenerates and behaves as a latch/current comparator with hysteresis, settling with one device near cutoff and the other in triode.

For ordinary saturated MOSFETs, \(g_mr_o\gg1\), so \(L\) is usually greater than one. Consequently, practical linear operation requires reducing the loop gain—by lowering \(g_mR\) products or adding sufficient conductance at \(X\)—or adding stabilizing negative feedback.

---

### 4. DC operating point

The general DC equations are

\[
I_{D2}=I_{\text{in}},\qquad
V_{\text{out}}=V_{DD}-R_{D1}I_{D1},
\]

with

\[
V_{GS1}=V_X,\quad V_{DS1}=V_{\text{out}},\qquad
V_{GS2}=V_{\text{out}},\quad V_{DS2}=V_X .
\]

If channel-length modulation is neglected and both devices are saturated, with \(\beta_i=\mu_nC_{\rm ox}(W/L)_i\),

\[
I_{\text{in}}
=\frac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{\text{out}}-V_{TH2})^2,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{V_{\text{out}}
=V_{TH2}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{\text{in}}}{\beta_2}}},
\qquad
\frac{dV_{\text{out}}}{dI_{\text{in}}}=\frac{1}{g_{m2}},
\]

and

\[
\boxed{
V_X=V_{TH1}
+\sqrt{\frac{2(V_{DD}-V_{\text{out}})}
{\beta_1R_{D1}}}
}.
\]

These equations locate the formal DC equilibrium or switching point. Since \(R_X\to\infty\) when \(\lambda=0\), \(L\to\infty\); this equilibrium is normally unstable and the actual large-signal circuit switches regeneratively.
